vision_features.image_context: Close-up ground-level view of a soybean plant at or near harvest maturity. Visible organs include pods (the dominant feature), stems, and a few remaining leaves. The image shows multiple plants at soil level with dried organic debris covering the ground.
vision_features.abnormalities: 1. Pods: The majority of pods visible are dry, papery, and tan-to-golden-brown in color, consistent with full maturity drying. Several pods appear twisted, shrunken, or slightly curled along their length. Some pods appear to have split or opened partially at the seams, with edges curling outward. The pod surfaces are covered in short, dense, light-colored (tan/golden) hair-like fibers, typical of soybean pods. A few pods show darker brown to nearly black discoloration patches on portions of their surface — these marks are irregular in shape, small to medium in size, and appear dry and flat (not raised or sunken). These darker patches are distributed unevenly across various pods, appearing on the surface of approximately 20–30% of pods visible. 2. Stems: Stems are green to yellowish-green at the upper portions and tan-to-straw-colored at lower portions, with visible fine hairs. A thin, wiry, purple-to-violet stem (likely a weed vine) is visible running diagonally through the scene — it is approximately 1–2 mm in diameter, smooth, and lacks the hairy texture of the soybean stems. 3. Leaves: A few leaves remain — some are pale green and appear wilted or flattened against the ground; one leaf (lower left) is still relatively green but drooping. Most leaves have dropped or are shriveled and brown among the ground debris. The fallen/dried leaf debris on the soil surface is uniformly tan-to-brown and papery.
vision_features.absences: 1. No visible powdery or dusty coating on any pod or leaf surfaces. 2. No raised bumps, pustules, or blister-like structures observed on the pod walls or stems. 3. No slimy, wet, or water-soaked tissue visible anywhere in the image. 4. No visible insect bodies, frass, or feeding damage holes on the pods or remaining leaves.
vision_features.summary: The image shows soybean plants at late maturity with predominantly dry, tan-to-golden-brown hairy pods, many of which are twisted, shrunken, or beginning to split open along their seams. Ground debris of fallen dry leaves covers the soil beneath the plants. A thin, smooth, purple-colored weed stem is intertwined among the soybean stems. A minority of pods display small, irregular dark brown patches on their surfaces, which are dry and flat in texture. The pods are the most prominently affected organ, and the most striking visual feature is the overall advanced drying and partial opening of the pods combined with the intrusion of the distinctive purple weed stem.

Knowledge-base entry for 'Phyllosticta_leaf_spot':
────────────────────────────────────────
Lesions most often occur on leaves and are circular, oval, and irregular or V-shaped. Lesions appear gray or tan and have a narrow, dark margin. Irregularly shaped tan/brownish lesions with purplish margins may be observed in the lower canopy.. In older lesions, numerous small, black specks (i.e., pycnidia) may be visible.
────────────────────────────────────────

Knowledge-base entry for 'Phytophthora':
────────────────────────────────────────
Young plants show rapid yellowing and wilting with soft rot and collapse of the root. Mature plants exhibit general yellowing of lower leaves progressing upward, followed by wilting and death, with brown discolored roots and a dark chocolate-brown stem discoloration extending from below the soil line upward several nodes; leaves typically stay attached after plant death.. The best diagnostic symptom on susceptible varieties is a lower stem discoloration (dark chocolate-brown) that may extend several nodes up the stem. Root system shows lateral and branch roots almost completely discolored; tap roots with brown surface discoloration and tan to brown inner tissue discoloration. Leaves turn yellow, wilt, and typically stay attached after plant death.. stem canker, Pythium
────────────────────────────────────────

Knowledge-base entry for 'Tobacco_Streak_Virus':
────────────────────────────────────────
Symptoms include bud blight, shepherd's crooking, stunting, wilting, delayed maturity, bud and leaf proliferation, reduced pod number, discolored, distorted, and dead leaves, discoloration and dead streaks at nodes, dark spots on pods, and delayed seed development.. Pod lesions, proliferation of tissue, discoloration and dead streaks at nodes, dark spots on pods, and seed discoloration are characteristic features.
────────────────────────────────────────

DISCRIMINATING: 'Tobacco_Streak_Virus' vs 'Phyllosticta_leaf_spot'
Ruling feature : Presence of discrete leaf lesions with dark margins vs. systemic/structural symptoms (streaking, distortion, bud abnormalities)
Tobacco_Streak_Virus: Tobacco Streak Virus causes systemic symptoms: bud blight, shepherd's crooking, stunting, wilting, dead streaks at nodes, dark spots on pods, distorted/dead leaves, and tissue proliferation — no discrete, well-defined leaf lesions described.
Phyllosticta_leaf_spot: Phyllosticta leaf spot produces discrete circular, oval, or V-shaped lesions on leaves that are gray or tan with a narrow dark (or purplish) margin, often bearing small black pycnidia (fungal fruiting bodies) within older lesions.
Decision rule  : IF the plant shows discrete, circular-to-irregular tan/gray leaf lesions with a dark border and/or small black specks within the lesion, THEN suspect Phyllosticta leaf spot; IF symptoms include bud blight, shepherd's crooking, node streaking, pod spots, and systemic distortion without well-defined margined leaf spots, THEN suspect Tobacco Streak Virus.
